name: Make one synth epic-drum patch sound like an ensemble of drummers: copy it to about four instances on the same MIDI, give each a different global decay, snap-EQ frequency and pan (about ±40), and add per-note random envelope delay (about 0-22 ms, tighten to about 7 ms, too loose at 65 ms) so the hits flam naturally. Optionally drive a filter with a tempo-synced step sequencer for rhythmic patterns
goal: Layer synthesized epic drums into a big, human-feeling ensemble quickly. Copying the same patch and MIDI usually just sounds like one louder hit. Put a few macro controls on the patch (global decay, snap frequency, global pitch, timing randomness) so each copy differs with a few slider moves, instead of editing each synth and the MIDI by hand.
prerequisites: A synthesized drum patch (noise/oscillator hit with amp and filter envelopes; see the epic hybrid drum skill)
A synth or host with macros, per-note random modulation and a tempo-synced step-sequencer LFO
A DAW that can duplicate tracks and MIDI

inputs.name: pattern
inputs.description: Simple rhythm pattern to copy to every instance

outputs.name: ensemble_drums
outputs.description: Four or so differentiated drum layers on shared MIDI

constraints: Original synthesis recipe; not affiliated with any vendor named in the source. Recreate in browser/Web Audio (Polyrhythm Studio) or any hybrid synth with comparable modules; no presets, banks or samples copied.
Vendor synth named in the video is mapped to generic macros and modulators.
Matt prefers steady pitch: keep per-hit random pitch off or very small. Use timing (envelope delay), decay, snap EQ and pan for variety, and use a fixed global pitch offset per layer instead.
Drums should enter early in Matt's tracks; this ensemble is a good early-entry layer if kept quiet at first.

Web Audio mapping: per voice, schedule start time = t + random(0, maxJitter) with maxJitter about 0.007-0.022 s, use a per-layer decay multiplier and pan via StereoPannerNode, and drive a BiquadFilter frequency from a tempo-locked step array.
Auto-generated YouTube Show transcript; values are as spoken and approximate where the speaker says 'about' or 'around'.

steps.action: Add macros to the patch: global decay (amp-env and filter-env decay together), snap frequency (a peaking EQ band on the attack), global pitch in semitones (about ±4) and randomness depth.
steps.expect: Four or five sliders that change each layer's character

steps.action: Add a per-note random modulator (new value on every MIDI note) on the amp-envelope delay and filter-envelope delay. Range about 0-22 ms at 50% randomness; 100% gives about 0-65 ms (too loose), and about 9% gives about 7 ms (tight).
steps.expect: Each hit starts slightly late by a random amount

steps.action: Write a simple pattern on instance 1, then duplicate the instance and its MIDI about three times.
steps.expect: Four identical layers (still sounds like one hit)

steps.action: On each copy, move the macros differently: decay up or down, snap frequency up or down, randomness slightly different, small fixed pitch offset. Pan pairs about 39-40 left and right.
steps.expect: Copies separate into audibly distinct drummers across the stereo field

steps.action: Listen and tighten: if a layer is too loose, lower its randomness (for example 86 to 68, 90 to 60).
steps.expect: Big flammed ensemble that still lands on the beat

steps.action: Optional rhythmic variant: an arpeggiator on eighth notes or a tempo-synced step-sequencer LFO driving the filter cutoff range. Change the step pattern or rate (8 to 16 steps, double speed) for new grooves. Lengthen the attack to turn hits into reverse-drum or noise-sweep textures.
steps.expect: Rhythmic drum sequences and swells from the same patch

verification: Four layers on identical MIDI produce audibly separate onsets (about 0-22 ms spread), not one summed hit.
No layer drifts more than about 25 ms from the grid after tightening.
Layers are panned about ±40 and differ in decay/brightness on solo comparison.
Per-hit pitch variation is zero or under about 0.5 semitone.
